# Answer key — Chapter 03: Web services, load and denial of service {.unnumbered}

<!-- Source-only: this directory is excluded from the render in _quarto.yml
     ("!answers/"). Never link these files from a chapter. Numbering must
     match the chapter's Self-check section 1:1. -->

**Q1** *(tests @sec-03-web-services-capacity · basic)* — **Correct: b.**
@def-capacity states that capacity is "established by measurement rather
than estimation", and @sec-03-measuring-load pushes the service until it
strains; hardware specs, SLAs and worker counts do not reveal where a
specific service's wall stands.

**Q2** *(tests @sec-03-denial-of-service · basic)* — **Correct: b.**
Protocol attacks exhaust connection state in servers or firewalls, the
classic case being the SYN flood, measured in packets per second
(@sec-03-denial-of-service). Volumetric attacks saturate the link,
application-layer attacks exhaust the application, and amplification is a
volumetric technique, not one of the three types.

**Q3** *(tests @sec-03-scaling-out · basic)* — **Correct: b.**
The chapter: a cluster of identical servers behind a load balancer, and
scaling out with many commodity machines proved cheaper and more resilient
than scaling up (@sec-03-scaling-out). Option a inverts the claim, c
contradicts the balancer's resilience role, and d contradicts the
interchangeable instances that enable autoscaling.

**Q4** *(tests @sec-03-sla · basic)* — **Accepted answers:**
"Chaining multiplies the availabilities, and a product of percentages below
100 % is lower than any factor", "every request needs all components, so
their availabilities multiply and the combined SLA drops below each single
component" (any phrasing naming multiplication of availabilities /
every-component-needed, per @sec-03-sla and @exm-compositesla).

**Q5** *(tests @sec-03-minimum-viable-network · basic)* — **Accepted
answers:** "Each tier accepts connections only from the tier directly above
it, and only on the ports that tier uses; everything not explicitly
permitted is dropped", "only the tier above, on its ports; the rest is
dropped (default-deny)" (must name the tier-above rule and the drop of
everything else).

**Q6** *(tests @sec-03-laboratory · basic)* — **Correct: c.**
The chapter states that the load-testing tool `ab` ships with Apache's
utilities, which is why `apache2-utils` is installed even to test Nginx
(@sec-03-laboratory). The other options invent dependencies the chapter
does not make.

**Q7 — applied scenario** *(tests @sec-03-defending-in-layers · applied)* —
**Model answer:** This is an application-layer flood, so the customer's own
configuration carries the weight (@sec-03-defending-in-layers). Two
server-side controls: (1) rate limiting with the Nginx `limit_req`
directive — caps requests per client and so blunts the flood at the point
where the cost arises; (2) caching — serves repeated content cheaply and
raises the effective capacity of the expensive search path (timeouts and
connection limits also acceptable — they stop slow or stuck clients from
hoarding state). Verification with the measurement tools of
@sec-03-measuring-load: re-run `ab` against the endpoint and compare the
failed-request count and requests-per-second/time-per-request figures before
and after; watch CPU/memory in `htop`/`btop` stay below the wall; check
`/var/log/nginx/access.log` for the capped/rejected requests. **Grading
notes:** full credit needs two correct customer-side controls including
`limit_req`, a per-control explanation tied to the application-layer type,
and at least two concrete pieces of verification evidence (`ab` report,
`htop`, access log). Partial credit for controls without verification, or
for edge/cloud controls only (those are the wrong side of the split for
this question).

## Sketch answers to the chapter exercises

(1) *(@exr-03-load-security-bridge — The load–security bridge)*
A denial-of-service attack is demand engineered to exceed capacity;
capacity depends on hardware, configuration and content, so only a controlled
load test reveals where a specific service's wall stands.

(2) *(@exr-03-apachebench-command — Reading an ApacheBench command)*
Send 2000 requests, 100 concurrently, to the local server; observe requests
per second, time per request, and the share of failed requests.

(3) *(@exr-03-three-ddos-types — The three DDoS types)*
Volumetric (UDP flood/amplification), protocol (SYN flood), application-layer
(flooding a search endpoint); the application layer is hardest to tell apart
because each request resembles a real user, so only patterns in the logs
reveal it.

(4) *(@exr-03-composite-sla — Computing a composite SLA)*
$0.9995 \times 0.9995 \times 0.995 \approx 0.9940$ = 99.40 %; about
$0.60\,\% \times 8760 \approx 53$ hours per year.

(5) *(@exr-03-application-layer-flood — An application-layer flood)*
The application layer: `limit_req` caps requests per client; a CDN absorbs
volume but forwards plausible dynamic queries, so the expensive endpoint
still burns, and the rate limit (plus caching) must sit where the cost
arises.
